newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin keeping work down, sends daughter on visit.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin keeping work down, sends daughter on visit.

text.p: The Kremlin said on Friday President Boris Yeltsin was strictly following doctor's orders by limiting his workload before planned heart surgery, but rapped the Western media over coverage of his illness.

Yeltsin's press secretary, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, said the president was working two to three hours a day at Moscow's Central Clinical Hospital and there were no immediate plans to change the schedule.
"Work with documents will be continued for two to three hours a day. The president will also have meetings on an individual basis when necessary," Yastrzhembsky told reporters.
Confined to the clinic, Yeltsin sent his daughter Tatyana on one of her first public engagements on his behalf on Friday. She flew to Rostov to visit children hurt in a school bus crash.

On Saturday, keeping up a modest workload, Yeltsin is due to meet his defence minister, Igor Rodionov, for talks on the problems facing the country's hard-up armed forces and the options for military reform, Russian news agencies reported.
Earlier this week Kremlin security chief Alexander Lebed warned the army may be on the verge of mutiny over unpaid wages.

Yeltsin may also debrief Rodionov on his meeting with NATO ministers in Norway this week. Russia is putting up resistance to the western defence alliance's plans for expansion in eastern Europe. Yeltsin confirmed on Friday that the tough-talking Lebed would visit NATO headquarters in Brussels on October 6 to 9.

Doctors said on Wednesday that Yeltsin, 65, was fit enough for a heart operation, but that surgery would be postponed for at least six weeks. The operation -- a relatively routine bypass operation -- will improve the blood supply to Yeltsin's heart.
In his prolonged absence, Lebed and communist leader Gennady Zyuganov have suggested instability and chaos could be looming.

Yeltsin announced his decision to undergo heart surgery in a television interview on September 5, breaking a long Kremlin tradition of secrecy about the health of Russian leaders. He has been in hospital since September 13.
Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin's health problems were no longer taboo but urged the media, particularly Western journalists, to respect "a certain framework of dignity and ethics".

"Sometimes I feel like asking you to spare the president, especially the Western media...I believe that -- this is my personal view -- the Western mass media have been using double standards in covering the president's illness," he said.
Yeltsin had two heart attacks last year and doctors say he may have had another one -- which the Kremlin concealed -- just before he was reelected for a new four-year term last July.

As Lebed and other senior officials maneouvred for position, Yeltsin sent his daughter Tatyana to the southern city of Rostov to visit the injured and convey his condolences to families of 17 children killed when a train hit their school bus.
Tatyana, 36, played a key role in Yeltsin's campaign and is an increasingly influential figure in his entourage but had kept very much in the background before his latest spell in hospital.
She gave her first major television interview last Sunday. Yeltsin's doctor said this week she visits her father every day.

Lebed and Zyuganov said on Thursday problems were piling up in Russia and action was needed. Zyuganov said Yeltsin should resign while the communist speaker of Russia's parliament renewed the opposition's criticism of the 1997 state budget.
Lebed got down to tackling one of the major problems, the conflict in breakaway Chechnya, by flying to the Ingushetia region of southern Russia for talks with regional leaders.
Chechen separatist leaders expressed their satisfaction with the talks and repeated their support for Lebed's peace moves.
